{{Short description|Line segment joining a triangle's vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side}}
{{distinguish|Geometric median}}
[[Image:Triangle.Centroid.Median.png|right|thumb|The triangle medians and the [[centroid]] O]]

In [[geometry]], a '''median''' of a [[triangle]] is a [[line segment]] joining a [[vertex (geometry)|vertex]] to the [[midpoint]] of the opposite side, thus bisecting that side. Every triangle has exactly three medians, one from each vertex, and they all intersect at the triangle's [[triangle centroid|centroid]]. In the case of [[isosceles]] and [[equilateral]] triangles, a median [[angle bisector|bisects any angle]] at a vertex whose two adjacent sides are equal in length.
The concept of a median extends to [[tetrahedron|tetrahedra]].

==Relation to center of mass==
Each median of a triangle passes through the triangle's [[centroid]], which is the [[center of mass]] of an infinitely thin object of uniform density coinciding with the triangle.<ref>{{cite book|last=Weisstein|first=Eric W.|title=CRC Concise Encyclopedia of Mathematics, Second Edition|year=2010|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=9781420035223|pages=375–377}}</ref> Thus, the object would balance at the intersection point of the medians. The centroid is twice as close along any median to the side that the median intersects as it is to the vertex it emanates from.

==Equal-area division==
Each median divides the area of the triangle in half, hence the name. (This equal area division does not by itself guarantee that the medians converge at the centroid.  Any other lines that divide a triangle's area into two equal parts do not pass through the centroid, and in general the triangle would not balance on a line simply because it divides the triangle into two parts of equal area.)<ref name=Bottomley2002>{{cite web |last=Bottomley |first=Henry |title=Medians and Area Bisectors of a Triangle
|url=http://www.se16.info/js/halfarea.htm |access-date=27 September 2013
|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190510194353/http://www.se16.info/js/halfarea.htm
|archive-date=2019-05-10
}}</ref><ref name=Dunn>Dunn, J. A., and Pretty, J. E., "Halving a triangle," ''[[Mathematical Gazette]]'' 56, May 1972, 105-108. DOI [https://doi.org/10.2307/3615256 10.2307/3615256] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230405215121/https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/mathematical-gazette/article/abs/halving-a-triangle/3765EE3B46D4C12F19B5259893164B11 |date=2023-04-05 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Hammoudeh |first=Ismail |date=2010 |title=Triangle Area Bisectors |url=https://demonstrations.wolfram.com/TriangleAreaBisectors/ |website=Wolfram Demonstrations Project |location= |publisher=Wolfram |access-date=5 August 2025}}</ref> The three medians divide the triangle into six smaller triangles of equal [[area]].

===Proof of equal-area property===
Consider a triangle ''ABC''. Let ''D'' be the midpoint of <math>\overline{AB}</math>, ''E'' be the midpoint of <math>\overline{BC}</math>, ''F'' be the midpoint of <math>\overline{AC}</math>, and ''O'' be the centroid (most commonly denoted ''G'').

By definition, <math>AD=DB, AF=FC, BE=EC </math>. Thus <math>[ADO]=[BDO], [AFO]=[CFO], [BEO]=[CEO],</math> and <math>[ABE]=[ACE] </math>, where <math>[ABC]</math> represents the [[area]] of triangle <math>\triangle ABC</math> ; these hold because in each case the two triangles have bases of equal length and share a common altitude from the (extended) base, and a triangle's area equals one-half its base times its height.

We have:
:<math>[ABO]=[ABE]-[BEO] </math>

:<math>[ACO]=[ACE]-[CEO] </math>

Thus, <math>[ABO]=[ACO] </math> and <math>[ADO]=[DBO], [ADO]=\frac{1}{2}[ABO]</math>

Since <math>[AFO]=[FCO], [AFO]= \frac{1}{2}[ACO]=\frac{1}{2}[ABO]=[ADO]</math>, therefore, <math>[AFO]=[FCO]=[DBO]=[ADO]</math>.
Using the same method, one can show that <math>[AFO]=[FCO]=[DBO]=[ADO]=[BEO]=[CEO] </math>.

===Three congruent triangles===
In 2014 [[Lee Sallows]] discovered the following theorem:<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sallows |first=Lee |date=2014 |title=A Triangle Theorem |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.4169/math.mag.87.5.381 |journal=Mathematics Magazine |volume=87 |issue=5 |pages=381 |doi=10.4169/math.mag.87.5.381 |issn=0025-570X}}</ref>
:The medians of any triangle dissect it into six equal area smaller triangles as in the figure above where three adjacent pairs of triangles meet at the midpoints D, E and F. If the two triangles in each such pair are rotated about their common midpoint until they meet so as to share a common side, then the three new triangles formed by the union of each pair are congruent.

==Formulas involving the medians' lengths==
The lengths of the medians can be obtained from [[Apollonius' theorem]] as:{{anchor|Length of a median expressed in terms of lengths of sides}}
<math display="block">m_a = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2 b^2 + 2 c^2 - a^2}</math>
<math display="block">m_b = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2 a^2 + 2 c^2 - b^2}</math>
<math display="block">m_c = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2 a^2 + 2 b^2 - c^2}</math>
where <math>a, b,</math> and <math>c</math> are the sides of the triangle with respective medians <math>m_a, m_b,</math> and <math>m_c</math> from their midpoints.

These formulas imply the relationships:{{anchor|Length of a side expressed in terms of lengths of medians}}<ref>{{cite book|last=Déplanche|first=Y.|title=Diccio fórmulas|others=Medianas de un triángulo|year=1996|publisher=Edunsa|isbn=978-84-7747-119-6|page=22|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1HVHOwAACAAJ|access-date=2011-04-24}}</ref>
<math display="block">a = \frac{2}{3} \sqrt{-m_a^2 + 2m_b^2 + 2m_c^2} = \sqrt{2(b^2+c^2)-4m_a^2} = \sqrt{\frac{b^2}{2} - c^2 + 2m_b^2} = \sqrt{\frac{c^2}{2} - b^2 + 2m_c^2}</math>
<math display="block">b = \frac{2}{3} \sqrt{-m_b^2 + 2m_a^2 + 2m_c^2} = \sqrt{2(a^2+c^2)-4m_b^2} = \sqrt{\frac{a^2}{2} - c^2 + 2m_a^2} = \sqrt{\frac{c^2}{2} - a^2 + 2m_c^2}</math>
<math display="block">c = \frac{2}{3} \sqrt{-m_c^2 + 2m_b^2 + 2m_a^2} = \sqrt{2(b^2+a^2)-4m_c^2} = \sqrt{\frac{b^2}{2} - a^2 + 2m_b^2} = \sqrt{\frac{a^2}{2} - b^2 + 2m_a^2}.</math>

==Other properties==

Let ''ABC'' be a triangle, let ''G'' be its centroid, and let ''D'', ''E'', and ''F'' be the midpoints of ''BC'', ''CA'', and ''AB'', respectively. For any point ''P'' in the plane of ''ABC'' then<ref>Problem 12015, American Mathematical Monthly, Vol.125, January 2018, DOI: 10.1080/00029890.2018.1397465</ref> 
<math display="block">PA+PB+PC \leq 2(PD+PE+PF) + 3PG.</math>

The centroid divides each median into parts in the ratio 2:1, with the centroid being twice as close to the midpoint of a side as it is to the opposite vertex.

For any triangle with sides <math>a, b, c</math> and medians <math>m_a, m_b, m_c,</math><ref name=P&S>Posamentier, Alfred S., and Salkind, Charles T., ''Challenging Problems in Geometry'', Dover, 1996: pp. 86–87.</ref>  
<math display="block">\tfrac{3}{4}(a+b+c) < m_a + m_b + m_c < a+b+c \quad \text{ and } \quad \tfrac{3}{4}\left(a^2+b^2+c^2\right) = m_a^2 + m_b^2 + m_c^2.</math>

The medians from sides of lengths <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> are [[perpendicular]] if and only if <math>a^2 + b^2 = 5c^2.</math><ref>Boskoff, Homentcovschi, and Suceava (2009), ''Mathematical Gazette'', Note 93.15.</ref>

The medians of a [[right triangle]] with hypotenuse <math>c</math> satisfy <math>m_a^2 + m_b^2 = 5m_c^2.</math>

Any triangle's area ''T'' can be expressed in terms of its medians <math>m_a, m_b</math>, and <math>m_c</math> as follows. If their semi-sum <math>\left(m_a + m_b + m_c\right)/2</math> is denoted by <math>\sigma</math> then<ref>Benyi, Arpad, "A Heron-type formula for the triangle", ''Mathematical Gazette'' 87, July 2003, 324–326.</ref>
<math display="block">T = \frac{4}{3} \sqrt{\sigma \left(\sigma - m_a\right)\left(\sigma - m_b\right)\left(\sigma - m_c\right)}.</math>

==Tetrahedron==
[[File:Tetrahedron centroid gimp.png|thumb|upright=1.25|{{center|medians of a tetrahedron}}<br/><math>\begin{align}&\frac{|AS|}{|SS_{BCD}|}=\frac{|BS|}{|SS_{ACD}|}=\frac{|CS|}{|SS_{ABD}|}\\[4pt]={}&\frac{|DS|}{|SS_{ABC}|}=\frac{3}{1} \end{align}</math>]]
A [[tetrahedron]] is a [[three-dimensional space|three-dimensional]] object having four triangular [[face (geometry)|faces]]. A line segment joining a vertex of a tetrahedron with the [[centroid]] of the opposite face is called a ''median'' of the tetrahedron. There are four medians, and they are all [[Concurrent lines|concurrent]] at the ''centroid'' of the tetrahedron.<ref>Leung, Kam-tim; and Suen, Suk-nam; "Vectors, matrices and geometry", Hong Kong University Press, 1994, pp. 53–54</ref> As in the two-dimensional case, the centroid of the tetrahedron is the [[center of mass]]. However contrary to the two-dimensional case the centroid divides the medians not in a 2:1 ratio but in a 3:1 ratio ([[Commandino's theorem]]).
